Modified assessment incorporating SLOOS evidence:
The April 29, 2020 FOMC statement is already strongly negative on growth, employment, and inflation, but the April 2020 SLOOS indicates an additional drag from bank credit that deepens the downside risks. Banks reported broad-based tightening of lending standards and terms—especially for C&I and CRE loans—wider rate spreads and higher costs of credit lines, and reduced risk tolerance tied to the COVID-19 shock. Demand weakened notably for CRE (nonfarm nonresidential, construction/land development), while some pockets (government residential mortgages) saw firmer demand and occasional easing/unchanged standards. On net, SLOOS implies tighter credit supply and softer credit demand that would amplify the downturn and partially counteract the Fed’s supportive stance (zero rates, open-ended Treasury/MBS purchases, large-scale repo).

SLOOS highlights relevant to this assessment:
- Tightened standards and terms: C&I (including middle market), CRE (nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily, construction/land development), HELOCs; wider loan rate spreads and higher premiums; increased costs of credit lines.
- Reasons cited: COVID-19, weaker economic outlook, industry-specific problems, reduced risk tolerance, liquidity needs; CRE concerns (property prices, cap rates, vacancy rates).
- Demand: Weaker for CRE and certain sectors; stronger for government residential mortgages; some increase in inquiries but banks focused less on new clients; banks expected further tightening ahead.

Implication: Relative to the FSR-only view, SLOOS points to a more restrictive bank-intermediated credit channel in the near term, reinforcing downside growth risks despite credible policy backstops. Accordingly, the sentiment is revised modestly more negative.
